actors.name: Chilean ATM gas and explosive attack crews
actors.description: Crews attacking ATMs in Chile using gas saturation and controlled explosion, a technique that resurged after roughly a decade of suppression. The tradecraft has since been observed being exported by Chilean nationals to Colombia, which makes this a genuinely transnational cluster rather than a national one.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: Directly relevant to Chilean and Andean ATM estates, and a clear illustration of how removing a control invites the attack back: Chilean banks had abandoned dye staining as ineffective before the resurgence. Cross-border export of the technique means neighbouring markets should treat Chilean incidence as a leading indicator.

actors.name: US hook-and-chain and smash-and-grab ATM removal crews
actors.description: Crews that back a pickup truck or SUV to an ATM, attach a chain, and pull the machine out of the ground or the storefront, loading it for later opening. actors.financial_sector_relevance: The most common destructive attack on the US ATM estate, and a substantial property damage and business interruption cost for host merchants as well as deployers. Anti-ram protection and floor anchoring are the primary controls, and the crews reliably migrate to the softest estate in a region.

actors.name: ATM technician ambush and induced-callout crews
actors.description: A refinement of jugging in which the crew deliberately disables an ATM, typically by injecting adhesive into the card reader or dispenser, waits for the servicing technician to arrive and open the safe, and then robs them at the open machine. It inverts the defender's assumption that the vulnerable moment is unscheduled; here the attacker chooses the timing.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: Turns the maintenance process itself into the attack vector, and defeats controls built around unpredictable replenishment schedules. Mitigation is procedural rather than physical: dual attendance on induced callouts, delay before opening a machine reported as tampered, and treating adhesive faults as a security event rather than a maintenance one.

actors.name: Air cargo and bullion insider-facilitated theft cluster
actors.description: Theft of high-value cargo, principally bullion and foreign currency, from airport cargo facilities using insider access and forged documentation rather than force. The April 2023 Toronto Pearson theft of over CAD 20 million in gold and foreign currency, executed with a fraudulent airway bill and the cooperation of airline employees, is the reference case; ten people were charged, including current and former airline staff.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: Bullion and currency shipments are a core banking logistics function and the weakest link is documentary control at the cargo handover, not the vault. It is also a striking insider case: the theft required no weapons, only a plausible document and someone willing to accept it. Recovered proceeds were minimal because the gold was melted down within days.

actors.name: Brazilian cash-in-transit and cash-logistics attack crews
actors.description: Crews that ambush armoured cash vehicles on highways and, in the highest-capability cases, attack cash vaults and airport cargo areas. The capability overlaps heavily with the PCC and with novo cangaco crews.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: Brazil operates one of the world's largest cash logistics markets, and CIT attack severity there sets the ceiling for what CIT operators globally must design against. Airport cargo attacks additionally implicate bullion and foreign currency movements handled by banks.

actors.name: Crypto kiosk-directed victim cluster
actors.description: Networks that direct scam victims, overwhelmingly older adults, to withdraw cash from their bank and deposit it into cryptocurrency kiosks under detailed instruction. The physical element is deliberate: cash withdrawal and kiosk deposit place the irreversible step outside the banking system. FBI IC3 recorded more than 13,400 complaints and over USD 388 million in losses in 2025, with 86 percent of losses among victims aged 60 and over.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: Places the bank branch and ATM at the centre of the intervention opportunity, because the withdrawal precedes the irreversible deposit. actors.name: North American electric grid physical attack cluster
actors.description: Physical attacks on electricity substations and distribution infrastructure in the United States and Canada, ranging from vandalism and copper theft through deliberate rifle fire into transformers to planned multi-site sabotage. DOE OE-417 reporting shows a pronounced rise: 25 actual physical attacks reported in 2022 against six in 2021, and by 2023 roughly 200 reports of vandalism, suspicious activity, sabotage or physical attack, some 58 percent of all reported disturbances, against 9.3 percent noting suspicious circumstances in 2017. Motivation is genuinely mixed, which is why this is coded hybrid: metal theft, grievance, curiosity and ideology all appear in the same statistics, and the reporting form does not distinguish them.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: Grid attack is the most concrete pathway by which a physical attack on someone else's asset takes a bank offline. Branch networks, ATM estates, data centres and payment processing all sit behind distribution infrastructure that is unfenced, unmonitored and legally protected only by ordinary criminal law. The Moore County attack took power from up to 40,000 customers for days, which is well beyond most institutions' generator autonomy and cash-resupply assumptions. It is also the clearest case in this database where an institution can measure its own exposure precisely, because OE-417 and EAGLE-I data are public and joinable to branch and data centre locations.

Cutting of perimeter fencing followed by damage to control cabinets and relays
Coordinated near-simultaneous attacks on multiple substations serving one area
Theft of copper grounding conductors, degrading protection systems
Arson against control houses and cable trenches
Reconnaissance of substation layout, sometimes by drone

financial_targeting.basis: No evidence of finance-specific targeting; exposure is downstream dependency on the affected grid segment.

actors.name: US jugging crews
actors.description: Crews, heavily associated with Houston-based street gangs but operating across state lines, that surveil banks and cash-heavy businesses, identify a customer or technician carrying cash, follow them and rob them. The mature form of the pattern targets ATM service technicians rather than retail customers, because a technician's vehicle carries cassette-level sums. Federal prosecutions in the Eastern and Northern Districts of Texas have established the model in detail.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: The most operationally significant physical threat to US cash servicing personnel. A technician can be followed across three or four cities before being robbed, meaning the attack happens far from the surveilled branch and outside its security perimeter. Sums involved reach a quarter of a million dollars per event, and the crews travel interstate specifically to defeat local pattern recognition.

actors.name: Mexican cobro de piso extortion cluster
actors.description: Systematic extortion of businesses by cartels, splinter groups and freelance criminals across most of Mexico, enforced by arson, kidnapping and murder. actors.name: Novo Cangaco raid crews
actors.description: A distinct Brazilian attack pattern in which a heavily armed crew seizes control of an entire small town for 20 to 60 minutes, neutralising police and communications, in order to strip its bank branches and ATMs. Crews are highly specialised, use assault rifles and explosives, and have taken an estimated USD 120 million since the pattern emerged in 2015. Some raids are attributable to the PCC; many are conducted by independent quadrilhas using the same doctrine.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: Defines the worst-case physical scenario for branch networks in low-density areas: the assumption that police response constrains attacker dwell time simply does not hold. It has driven Brazilian banks toward cashless branches, remote vault management and closure of rural cash points, which is itself a financial-inclusion consequence worth tracking.

actors.name: US armoured car and cash-logistics robbery cluster
actors.description: Crews that attack armoured car crews at the pavement transfer point, the moment when cash or valuables are outside the vehicle and the guard is exposed. Unlike the Italian or Brazilian pattern there is little use of explosives or heavy weapons; the US pattern is ambush at the point of transfer, frequently with inside information about the run. actors.name: Southern and Eastern European gas-mixture ATM attack crews
actors.description: Crews that saturate the ATM safe cavity with an oxygen-fuel gas mixture and detonate it, a cheaper and more widely available method than solid explosive. Composition of these crews varies by country: Romanian and Bulgarian nationals feature heavily in Iberian and Central European cases, local groups dominate in Italy and Greece. The technique persists because gas is legally purchasable and the required skill floor is low, but yields are lower and misfire rates higher than solid-charge attacks.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: Sustains a baseline of destructive ATM attacks across markets where explosive precursors are harder to source. Migration of crews between countries following successful national hardening programmes

actors.name: Netherlands-origin ATM solid-explosive attack crews
actors.description: Loosely federated crews, predominantly Dutch nationals from the greater Utrecht and Amsterdam areas, who attack through-the-wall and lobby ATMs with solid explosive charges. Dutch banks hardened their estate with ink/glue neutralisation and night-time cash withdrawal from machines, so the crews exported the tradecraft into North Rhine-Westphalia, Switzerland and eastern France. Crews are small (4-10), recruit young drivers via encrypted messaging, and use stolen high-powered vehicles for cross-border egress. Eurojust and Europol have run repeated joint actions against them; the model reconstitutes because the knowledge is commoditised and distributed as tutorials.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: Highest-frequency destructive physical attack on the European ATM estate. Attacks cause collateral structural damage to branch buildings and residential premises above them, drive up insurance and remediation cost far beyond cash loss, and create third-party fatality risk that carries direct liability for the deploying bank.

Cross-border operating pattern exploiting jurisdictional seams (NL-DE, DE-CH, FR-DE)

actors.name: Ram-raid and plant-machinery ATM removal crews
actors.description: Crews that steal agricultural or construction plant, most often telehandlers and excavators, and use it to rip through-the-wall ATMs and their safes out of building fabric, loading the whole unit into a waiting flatbed or 4x4. actors.name: Courier fraud gangs
actors.description: Crews that telephone elderly victims posing as police or bank fraud teams, persuade them that their account is compromised, and then dispatch a physical courier to collect cards, PINs, cash or gold from the doorstep. It is a hybrid by construction: the deception is remote, but the value extraction requires a person to attend an address, which is also the point at which the crews are most detectable. UK losses exceed GBP 21 million a year.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: Places a criminal physically at the customer's door on the strength of an impersonated bank identity, and frequently walks the victim into a branch to make a withdrawal the branch has no obvious reason to refuse. actors.name: European crypto wrench-attack crews
actors.description: Crews that abduct, restrain or invade the homes of cryptocurrency holders and executives and coerce transfers of keys or funds. France has become the global epicentre: at least 41 crypto-related kidnappings and home invasions were reported in a single year, and prosecutors charged 88 people, including minors, in a coordinated crackdown. Crew composition is notably unprofessional, which raises rather than lowers the risk of serious injury.

Home invasion or street abduction with restraint of family members

actors.description: Organised crews, concentrated in London but replicated in Paris, Barcelona and Amsterdam, that steal unlocked smartphones in the street and immediately exploit the open banking, payment and crypto apps on them. actors.description: Not a group but a persistent enabling pattern: organised crime networks recruit or coerce employees of banks, cash-in-transit operators, ATM service providers and their contractors to supply schedules, keys, alarm states, customer data and access. actors.name: ATM jackpotting and black-box attack crews
actors.description: Crews that open the ATM top box, disconnect the dispenser from the core, attach an unauthorised controller (black box) or install malware, and command a full cash-out. This is the archetypal hybrid attack: physical access is the enabler, software is the payload. European incidence has fallen sharply with dispenser-authentication and hard-disk encryption rollouts, but the technique persists against legacy estates and re-emerges wherever an operator defers firmware upgrades.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: Directly demonstrates why ATM physical security and endpoint security cannot be governed separately. A successful jackpot empties every cassette without any building damage, so it is often detected only at reconciliation.

Disconnection of the dispenser and attachment of an unauthorised controller
Deployment of dispenser-targeting malware via USB or exposed ports

Use of money mules to collect dispensed cash within a short window

actors.description: Profit-driven crews that strip copper cable, earthing conductors and metal from telecoms, rail and power infrastructure. actors.name: NFC data-relay and terminal-proximity fraud cluster
actors.description: The fastest-growing physical-adjacent attack on European payment terminals. Compromised card credentials are provisioned into a wallet on an operator-controlled handset; a mule then presents that handset at a genuine terminal, with relay software bridging the NFC exchange to a device held elsewhere. It converts remote credential theft into card-present transactions at physical merchants, which is why it belongs in a physical threat model rather than a purely cyber one.

Geographic dispersal of taps to stay under velocity thresholds

actors.name: Shadow-fleet subsea cable interference cluster
actors.description: Repeated damage to subsea telecommunications and power cables in the Baltic and North Sea, associated with vessels of Russia's sanctions-evasion shadow fleet and, in at least one case, a Chinese-registered ship. actors.description: Crews that abduct or hold the family of a bank, cash centre or CIT employee overnight, then compel that employee to remove cash the following morning. actors.description: Individuals with no prior intelligence relationship, recruited over Telegram and messaging apps and paid in cryptocurrency to conduct arson, reconnaissance, package placement and rail sabotage on behalf of Russian services. actors.name: GRU Unit 29155 / Department of Special Tasks

Realistic scenarios are not branch attacks but sabotage of the physical substrate finance depends on: power feeds, fibre routes, data centre supply chains and logistics nodes. actors.name: Branch siege, hostage and grievance-driven attack cluster
actors.description: Incidents in which an individual, usually acting alone and often a customer rather than a professional criminal, takes over a bank branch. actors.financial_sector_relevance: The scenario branch staff are most likely to actually face, and the one where security posture interacts most directly with reputational risk, because the assailant may be a sympathetic figure. actors.name: Cable landing station and terrestrial fibre chokepoint exposure
actors.description: The shore end of the subsea cable system: landing stations, beach manholes, terrestrial backhaul and the small number of geographic chokepoints where many cables converge. More than 150 cable faults occur worldwide each year, with fishing and anchoring accounting for close to 70 percent, so deliberate sabotage is a small minority of a large number. That statistic cuts both ways. It means most outages are accidental, and it means a deliberate cut is easy to hide inside the noise. Landing stations are a far softer target than the cable itself: they are on land, few in number, and often lightly guarded.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: Financial messaging, market data, inter-datacentre replication and cloud connectivity all depend on this infrastructure, and route diversity purchased from carriers frequently converges at the same landing station or the same duct without the buying institution knowing. That is the actual risk: not that a cable will be cut, but that an institution's documented diversity is fictional at the shore end. Repair timelines are governed by cable ship availability, which is a global constraint no customer can escalate.
ttps: Physical intrusion or damage at landing stations and beach manholes
Cutting of terrestrial backhaul in ducts and at aggregation points
Exploitation of chokepoints where many systems converge geographically
Concealment of deliberate damage within the high baseline of accidental faults
Targeting of repair and maintenance capacity, which is globally scarce

existence.basis: ICPC and carrier fault reporting; documented landing station security concerns in national reviews.

attribution.basis: Accidental and deliberate damage are difficult to distinguish; deliberate cases are rarely attributed.

financial_targeting.basis: Shared infrastructure with no finance-specific selection observed.

watch_indicators: Carrier fault notifications on routes carrying financial traffic

actors.name: Coerced-withdrawal and ATM duress cluster
actors.description: Offenders who abduct or restrain a victim and drive them between ATMs, forcing withdrawals up to daily limits, sometimes across a rollover at midnight to double the take. Repeated maximum withdrawals across multiple machines in a short window, especially spanning midnight, is a recognisable and actionable signature. Some institutions have implemented duress-aware limits and referral rules on this basis.

actors.name: Targeted violence against financial sector executives and staff
actors.description: A convergent pattern rather than a single actor: organised crime coercing compliance and investigations staff, ideologically motivated attacks on named executives, grievance-driven lone actors, and kidnapping of banking personnel for ransom in high-kidnap jurisdictions. Data protection of staff personal information is now a physical security control, not just a privacy one.

actors.name: Hardware and firmware supply-chain tampering cluster
actors.description: Physical modification of hardware or firmware somewhere between manufacture and deployment: implanted devices added to servers, network gear, ATMs, HSMs and payment terminals; firmware flashed during manufacture, repair or shipping interdiction; or rogue devices attached to a network by someone who walked in. This is the category where public claims and public evidence diverge most sharply. The 2018 Bloomberg Supermicro report remains unverified and denied by the named parties, and it merged a hardware claim, an actor claim and a tasking claim into a single assertion, which is precisely the failure mode this database's per-variable confidence model exists to avoid. Firmware compromise and rogue device addition, by contrast, are routinely demonstrated.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: Banks operate more security-critical hardware than almost any other commercial sector: HSMs, PIN pads, ATM dispensers and cash controllers, card personalisation equipment. Each has a supply chain, a repair loop and a decommissioning path, and each is handled by third parties. The realistic and demonstrated threats are firmware tampering during repair, terminal substitution in the field and rogue devices added inside offices. The exotic nation-state implant scenario absorbs disproportionate attention relative to its evidence base, and treating both at the same confidence level distorts spending.
ttps: Firmware modification during manufacture, repair or refurbishment
Interdiction and modification of equipment in shipping
Addition of rogue network devices by an insider or a visitor with premises access
Substitution of payment terminals and ATM components with modified units
Compromise of the vendor's own update and signing infrastructure
Exploitation of weak provenance controls in refurbished and grey-market hardware

existence.basis: Firmware tampering, rogue device addition and terminal substitution are well demonstrated; the server implant scenario is not.

attribution.basis: Very few incidents are attributed to a named actor; the most publicised claim remains unverified and denied.

financial_targeting.basis: ATM, HSM and payment terminal hardware is demonstrably targeted; general server implant targeting of finance is unevidenced.

state_tasking.basis: Asserted in reporting on the highest-profile case, never established.

actors.description: The physical movement of cash, gold and bearer value across borders by human couriers, vehicle concealment and air cargo, underpinning almost every laundering typology in this database. actors.name: Private security and cash-logistics industry infiltration cluster
actors.description: Deliberate placement or recruitment of personnel inside guarding companies, cash-in-transit operators and ATM service providers. actors.name: Accelerationist infrastructure-attack networks
actors.description: Transnational neo-Nazi accelerationist networks that promote attacks on electricity infrastructure as a deliberate strategy to precipitate societal collapse. The Terrorgram Collective functioned as a publishing and radicalisation layer rather than an operational cell structure, distributing target guidance and celebrating attacks. Its two US-based leaders were arrested in September 2024, and Atomwaffen Division founder Brandon Russell was convicted in February 2025 and sentenced in August 2025 to 20 years for conspiring to destroy electrical facilities serving Baltimore. More than a dozen separate federal prosecutions involve alleged core members or individuals inspired toward infrastructure attacks.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: Relevant in two ways, and it is worth being precise about which. Directly, the ideology is antisemitic and explicitly anti-financial, so banks appear in propaganda target lists alongside synagogues, power stations and data centres, and staff who are publicly identifiable are within the threat model. Indirectly and more probably, the strategy of attacking electricity infrastructure to induce cascading failure puts the institution's continuity planning, not its guard force, in the line of fire. Attack planning is amateur but intent is explicit and published, which makes it unusually legible for a threat of this severity.

Celebration of unattributed attacks to encourage imitation

actors.name: DPRK-linked coordinated ATM cash-out networks
actors.description: North Korean state-directed operations that compromise a bank's payment switch or card processing environment, force fraudulent authorisation responses, and then simultaneously withdraw cash from ATMs across many countries using pre-positioned mule networks. It is the purest hybrid in this database: the intrusion is remote and the extraction is entirely physical, requiring hundreds of people standing at machines in coordinated time windows. US CISA and Treasury have issued repeated advisories.

Detection depends on correlating switch anomalies with ATM withdrawal patterns in near real time, which requires the fraud, cyber and ATM operations functions to share telemetry. Losses are realised in minutes across dozens of jurisdictions and are effectively unrecoverable.

actors.name: State-sponsored OT pre-positioning in critical infrastructure
actors.description: PRC state-sponsored intrusion into the IT environments of communications, energy, transportation and water utilities, with US authoring agencies assessing with high confidence that the objective is pre-positioning for lateral movement into operational technology in order to disrupt functions during a future crisis. Tracked as Volt Typhoon by CISA and as VOLTZITE by Dragos, among numerous vendor names. It belongs in a physical threat database because the intended effect is physical: the loss of power, water or communications, not the theft of data.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: This is the case the Elephantine Void argument is really about. What is established is presence in utility IT networks and an assessed intent to reach OT. What is not established is any executed disruption, and conflating the two overstates the position. For a bank the practical exposure is identical to the grid attack cluster and should be planned for the same way, as dependency on utilities that may fail without warning and without a weather explanation. The distinctive addition is that a state-timed outage would be simultaneous across regions, which defeats mutual-aid and failover assumptions built around localised events.

Compromise of small office and edge network devices as operational relays
